newsitem.title: USA: FCC chief condemns AT&T-SBC merger.
newsitem.headline: FCC chief condemns AT&T-SBC merger.

text.p: The nation's top telephone regulator Thursday condemned a possible merger of AT&T Corp. and SBC Communications Inc., calling such a corporate marriage "unthinkable" and signalling his intent to block any deal.
Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt said such a combination, which would be the largest in U.S. history, would hurt competition and violate antitrust laws protecting consumers.

His views reflect growing alarm among government officials about the spree of mergers in the telecommunications business after last year's telecom law. Such worries could sink any AT&T-SBC deal, or similar deals being mulled for the future.
No. 1 long-distance carrier AT&T and regional Baby Bell giant SBC are believed to be in merger talks which, if completed, would amount to a $50 billion-plus transaction.
"A combination of AT&T and an RBOC (regional Bell operating company) is unthinkable," Hundt said in a speech at the Brookings Institution.
While Hundt did not refer specifically to AT&T and SBC, his comments clearly targeted such a combination.

AT&T Chairman Robert Allen -- while not mentioning an AT&T-SBC deal -- last week said in a speech that the possibility of a long-distance carrier merging with a Baby Bell could be "pro-competitive." He said it would be "not unthinkable."
But Hundt, a lawyer with 20 years of antitrust experience under his belt, said the resulting local and long-distance phone market power would be "unthinkable."

He said such a deal "would be exactly the type of ... combination that antitrust law frowns upon." The FCC chairman said regulators need to look at whether two companies naturally would be competitors if it were not for the artificial barriers in place before the 1996 telecom law.

Philip Verveer, an attorney with Willkie Farr & Gallagher who worked on the government's breakup of the old Ma Bell phone monopoly in 1984, said Hundt's speech could force any AT&T-SBC combination to be scuttled before it is announced.
"To carry on with this thing in the face of so forceful a statement would be remarkable," he said.
Although Hundt has announced plans to step down, the FCC chief has close ties to Vice Pesident Al Gore, and his thoughts are believed to reflect Clinton administration worries.

"He is not going to go this far out on a limb if he doesn't believe he has a lot of troops behind him," said analyst Scott Cleland of Legg Mason Precursor Group, the research arm of the Baltimore-based brokerage.
AT&T serves more than 80 million residential customers and 10 million businesses. SBC dominates local phone service in a seven-state area stretching from Texas to California.

AT&T Vice President Mark Rosenblum declined to confirm any merger talks. But he said regulators should consider any merger proposal that could spur competition in all markets across the country -- "when and if it is made."

"If a partnership between a long-distance company and a local RBOC can be structured to increase competition both in the RBOC's home territory and in the states it does not currently serve, then it ought to be considered," he said.
SBC declined to comment.
In an interview, Hundt told Reuters that government regulators need to let companies know ahead of time whether any potential merger has a chance of passing muster.
"We don't serve anyone's interest by putting our heads in the sand like the ostrich," he said. "The whole purpose of the Telecom Act was to get the FCC to lay out a blueprint for the future."
On Wall Street, AT&T's stock was up 12.5 cents at $37.625 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. SBC was up 25 cents at $60.50, also on the NYSE.
